title: What was the Four Pests Campaign?
summary: Josh and Chuck (Chuck is credited as the 'iHeart Intro' speaker in this transcript) explain the Four Pests Campaign, a 1958-1960s Maoist eradication drive in China targeting rats, mosquitoes, flies, and sparrows. They cover its roots in the Great Leap Forward, the propaganda used to mobilize people, Josh's back-of-envelope estimates of how many flies and mosquitoes were killed, the rat and sparrow kills, the ecological fallout (locust outbreaks after sparrows were nearly wiped out) and its link to the Great Famine of 1958-1961, the reversal after zoologist Zeng Zujin's research, later reboots including cockroaches in 1998 and later mosquito campaigns, and the lasting health effects of the famine. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about the Black Sabbath movie reference in the Heavy Metal episode.

segments.title: Introduction to the Four Pests Campaign
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic, suggested by listener Emily Bryant, and describe the four pests (rats, mosquitoes, flies, sparrows) targeted in communist China in the late 1950s and early 1960s.

segments.title: Earlier fly campaigns and the Great Leap Forward
segments.summary: Earlier Chinese fly-killing drives in the 1920s and 1930s are described, along with the 1958 Great Leap Forward goal of overtaking UK industrial output and the American newspaper's reaction to the campaign.

segments.title: Mao's drive to dominate nature
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Mao's slogan that man must conquer nature, his stated desire to make mountains bow and rivers yield, and the public health motives such as disease, infant mortality, and grain loss that justified targeting the pests.

segments.title: Sparrows as grain thieves and community participation
segments.summary: Estimates of grain losses blamed on sparrows are described, and the hosts explain how communities organized sanitation teams and individuals were urged to kill pests.

segments.title: Propaganda and public opinion
segments.summary: Government posters and children's songs and books promoted killing pests, with slogans about happiness for generations. The hosts note that public attitudes toward sparrows shifted quickly after the campaign began.

segments.title: Data reliability and Josh's fly math
segments.summary: The hosts caution that Chinese statistics and counts of individual insects are unreliable. Josh estimates the number of flies killed, roughly 220 million pounds, by converting weight to individual flies, arriving at trillions.

segments.title: Rats, mosquitoes, and their disease risks
segments.summary: Rats are discussed as carriers of disease and grain thieves, with about 1.5 billion killed by Josh's estimate of weight. Mosquito control methods are covered, including draining water, stocking fish and ducks to eat larvae, and insecticide fogging, plus a note on genetically modified mosquito proposals.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Sparrow killing methods and the locust problem
segments.summary: The methods used to kill sparrows are described, including banging pots and pans until birds dropped and destroying nests and eggs. Without sparrows, locusts thrived and devastated crops.

segments.title: Great Chinese Famine
segments.summary: The hosts link the campaign to the Great Famine of 1958 to 1961, estimated to have killed millions, and discuss Mao's denial and the blame placed on rightists. Other causes include drought, flooding, crop failure, and the Soviet Union's debt call-in claim.

segments.title: Backyard steel and grain export policies
segments.summary: Backyard steel furnaces produced poor pig iron, and farming was neglected. Grain quotas and reporting practices led to exports and rural starvation, and torture of dissenters contributed to deaths.

segments.title: Reversal on sparrows and Zeng Zujin's research
segments.summary: China removed sparrows from the Four Pests list after research showed they mostly eat insects, about 75 percent, and only eat grain in winter. Sparrows were then reintroduced from the Soviet Union and killing them was later outlawed.

segments.title: Later campaigns and lasting effects
segments.summary: Bed bugs replaced sparrows, cockroaches were added in a 1998 reboot, rat campaigns in the 1980s were large, mosquito campaigns continued with China declared malaria-free, and studies in 2023 found lasting health effects on famine survivors.

segments.title: Lon yap aside
segments.summary: Josh gives the Chinese word for sparrow, mache, and tells a story about the term lon yap, meaning an extra little treat.

segments.title: Listener mail on Black Sabbath movie
segments.summary: A listener from Brookline, New Hampshire, points out that a Boris Karloff movie called Black Sabbath is not about a talking boat winning a regatta for orphans, as Josh had said in the Heavy Metal episode. Josh admits he made up that plot.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite email. The show credits iHeartRadio.
